title: Saga & Process Managers
summary: Process managers/sagas coordinate multi-step business workflows across services with explicit state machines, timeouts, and compensations — a pattern-level view of distributed transactions.

sections.title: Process manager role
paragraphs: A process manager listens to events, advances a workflow state machine, and commands participants. It owns the workflow state, not the domain aggregates' invariants.

sections.title: State and timeouts
paragraphs: Persist workflow state. Timeouts trigger probes or compensations. Humans may be in the loop for exceptional paths.

sections.title: Implementation tips
paragraphs: Use durable workflow engines (Temporal, Cadence) or carefully built state machines. Exactly-once side effects still need idempotency keys.

sections.title: Anti-patterns
paragraphs: God orchestrators that encode all business logic. Prefer managers that coordinate while domains keep invariants.

deepDive.title: Saga & Process Managers — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Saga & Process Managers in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Saga & Process Managers — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Saga & Process Managers include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Saga & Process Managers — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Saga & Process Managers intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

keyTakeaways: Sagas are state machines with compensations
whyItMatters: Long-running business processes are everywhere in real systems.
reflectionQuestions: Where do you store workflow progress today?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
